Born in Butka and raised in Kazan and Berezniki, which one-time Communist Party official became the first President of Russia?
Boris Yeltsin (1 February 1931 - 23 April 2007) was a Soviet and Russian politician who served as President of Russia from 1991 to 1999.

In Greek mythology, this ferryman transported the souls of the properly buried dead across the river bordering the underworld, and demanded a coin placed in the mouth of each corpse as payment — who is he?
Charon (-n; Ancient) is the ferryman of the Greek underworld.
In Greek mythology, this skillful architect built the Labyrinth that imprisoned the Minotaur and later crafted wings so he and his son could flee Crete — who is he?
Daedalus was a skillful architect and craftsman, seen as a symbol of wisdom, knowledge and power.

A businessman who mortgaged inherited farmland in 1983 to fund a software startup, this politician served two terms as governor of North Dakota before becoming a US Cabinet secretary in 2025 — who is he?
Doug Burgum (born August 1, 1956) is an American businessman and politician who has served as the 55th United States secretary of the interior since 2025 under President Donald Trump.

French Revolution was a period of political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General of 1789 and ended with the Coup of 18 Brumaire on 9 November 1799.
Before becoming UK Prime Minister in 2007, this Labour politician spent a decade as Chancellor of the Exchequer under Tony Blair — who is he?
Gordon Brown (born 20 February 1951) is a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and Leader of the Labour Party from 2007 to 2010.

Historians often treat this ancient Semitic-speaking people as equivalent to another biblical group, with the name traditionally applied to their nomadic era before a kingdom arose in the 11th century BCE — who were they?
Hebrews (ISO 259-3: ibrim / ibriyim) were an ancient Semitic-speaking people.
Descended from the founder of the 18th-century Emirate of Diriyah and led today by the descendants of its modern founder, this is the ruling royal family of a Middle Eastern kingdom — which family?
House of Saud is the ruling royal family of Saudi Arabia.
Ruling from 1501 until his death in 1524, this Safavid founder unified Iran under native rule for the first time in over eight centuries — who was he?
Ismail I (17 July 1487 - 23 May 1524) was the founder and first shah of Safavid Iran, ruling from 1501 until his death in 1524.
A former Carlyle Group partner and investment banker, this attorney served as the 16th chair of the Federal Reserve from 2018 to 2026 — who is he?
Jerome Powell (born February 4, 1953) is an American central banker and attorney who served as the 16th chair of the Federal Reserve from 2018 to 2026.
Whose son Bernardo became President of Guatemala in 2024, decades after this philosophy-professor-turned-statesman first won the office democratically in 1945?
Juan José Arévalo (10 September 1904 - 8 October 1990) was a Guatemalan statesman and professor of philosophy who became Guatemala's first democratically elected president in 1945.

Splitting from the Kingdom of León in 1065, reuniting with it between 1072 and 1157, and permanently merging after 1230, this medieval Iberian realm led extensive conquests into Islamic-held southern Iberia — which kingdom?
Kingdom of Castile was a polity in the Iberian Peninsula during the Middle Ages.
The 1848 Democratic presidential nominee, this Michigan senator and Army officer became the leading spokesman for 'popular sovereignty' on slavery — which slave-owning statesman is it?
Lewis Cass (October 9, 1782 - June 17, 1866) was a United States Army officer and politician.
The first woman to serve as chief minister of West Bengal, this Indian politician founded her own party after breaking from the Indian National Congress in 1998 — who is she?
Mamata Banerjee (Bengali; born 5 January 1955) is an Indian politician and lawyer who served as the eighth chief minister of West Bengal from 2011 to 2026.
A radical Jacobin lawyer who campaigned for all men's voting rights and the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade, he joined the Committee of Public Safety in 1793 — who was he?
Maximilien Robespierre (6 May 1758 - 28 July 1794) was a French lawyer and statesman, widely recognised as one of the most influential figures of the French Revolution.

Commanding both the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Muslim Peshmerga during the Iran-Iraq War, this Iranian officer, who died in 1983, helped restore Iran's control over Kurdistan — who was he?
Mohammad Boroujerdi (1955 - 1983) was an Iranian commander in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps during the Iran-Iraq War.

This wealthy Republican politician served as governor of New York for 14 years before becoming the 41st U.S. vice president under Gerald Ford, lending his family name to a moderate wing of his party — who is he?
Nelson Rockefeller (July 8, 1908 - January 26, 1979) was the 41st vice president of the United States, serving from 1974 to 1977 under President Gerald Ford.
A member of the Bundestag since 2006 representing Hesse, this German-Iranian politician co-led Alliance 90/The Greens with Ricarda Lang and now serves as Vice President of the Bundestag — who is he?
Omid Nouripour (born 18 June 1975) is a German-Iranian politician who has been serving as Vice President of the Bundestag since 2025.
Writing independence tracts from Japan and later swayed by Sun Yat-sen toward republicanism, which Vietnamese revolutionary founded the Đông Du movement against French rule?
Phan Bội Châu (26 December 1867 - 29 October 1940) was a Vietnamese nationalist and revolutionary.
A businessman who became Lebanon's wealthiest politician, he helped forge the Taif Agreement ending the civil war and led the rebuilding of Beirut before his 2005 assassination — who was he?
Rafic Hariri (1 November 1944 - 14 February 2005) was a Lebanese businessman and politician who served as prime minister of Lebanon from 1992 to 1998 and again from 2000 to 2004.
A human-rights lawyer who rode a wave of younger internet users into office, he became South Korea's ninth president in 2003 — which leader of the so-called '386 Generation' was it?
Roh Moo-hyun (1 September 1946 - 23 May 2009) was a South Korean politician and lawyer who served as the ninth president of South Korea from 2003 to 2008.

A renowned scholar of comparative religion who held endowed chairs at Calcutta and Oxford, he climbed from ambassador to the Soviet Union all the way to the presidency of India — who was this philosopher-statesman?

Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan (5 September 1888 - 17 April 1975) was an Indian academic, philosopher and statesman who served as the Vice President of India from 1952 to 1962 and President of India from 1962 to 1967.
Born in a village near Vicenza, Italy, she took the helm of India's Congress party seven years after her husband's assassination and became its longest-serving president — who is she?
Sonia Gandhi (ne Maino; born 9 December 1946) is an Indian politician.
After meeting his co-conspirator during a brief Army stint, this domestic terrorist helped plan the 1995 truck bombing of a federal building in Oklahoma City — who is he?
Terry Nichols (born April 1, 1955) is an American domestic terrorist who was convicted for conspiring with Timothy McVeigh in the Oklahoma City bombing plot.
In Norse mythology, these female figures choose which slain warriors are worthy to be guided to Odin's hall, where they serve the fallen mead between preparations for Ragnarök — what are they called?
Valkyrie (or val-; from Old Norse valkyrja, lit. 'chooser of the slain') is one of a host of female figures who guide souls of the dead to the god Odin's hall Valhalla.
The first French Canadian to lead the country, this prime minister built his reputation on compromises between English and French Canada and served an unbroken 15 years — who was he?
Wilfrid Laurier (November 20, 1841 - February 17, 1919) was the seventh prime minister of Canada from 1896 to 1911.
This career U.S. Army officer became a national hero in the Mexican-American War, rode that fame to the White House as the 12th president, and died just 16 months into his term — who is he?
Zachary Taylor (November 24, 1784 - July 9, 1850) was the 12th president of the United States, serving from 1849 until his death in 1850.

Andrés Manuel López Obrador: President of Mexico from 2018 to 2024. This legal process lasted a year, ending with López Obrador maintaining his right to run for office.

This Republican politician served as Arkansas's governor from 2015 to 2023 after earlier stints as a US attorney and member of Congress, and later ran for the 2024 GOP presidential nomination. Who is he?

Asa Hutchinson: Governor of Arkansas from 2015 to 2023. In 1982, President Ronald Reagan appointed Hutchinson to serve as the U.S. attorney for the Western District of Arkansas, which covers most of Fort Smith.

Sparked partly by Emperor Hadrian's plan to rebuild Jerusalem as a Roman colony dedicated to Jupiter, this 132–136 CE uprising was the last and most devastating of the major Jewish rebellions against Rome, leading to Judea's near-total depopulation — which uprising was it?
Bar Kokhba Revolt: Jewish rebellion against Roman rule (132–136 CE)
Active in local politics in Corrèze, this Frenchwoman spent 25 years heading a children's charity while her husband occupied the presidential palace — who was she?

Catherine of Aragon: Queen of England from 1509 to 1533.

Christian IX: King of Denmark from 1863 to 1906.

Domitian: Roman emperor from AD 81 to 96.

Efraín Ríos Montt: 38th President of Guatemala from 1982 to 1983.
This Turkish socialist academic-turned-politician leads the Workers' Party of Turkey and represents Istanbul in parliament — who is he?

Fernando Henrique Cardoso: President of Brazil from 1995 to 2003.

French First Republic: Three regimes of revolutionary and early Napoleonic France (1792–1804)

Harald Bluetooth: 10th-century King of Denmark and Norway. Harald "Bluetooth" Gormsson (Old Norse: Haraldr Blátǫnn Gormsson; Danish: Harald Blåtand Gormsen, died c. 985/86) was a king of Denmark and Norway.
Coined by a 12th-century historian, this term describes Anglo-Saxon England's traditional division into seven petty kingdoms like Wessex, Mercia, and Kent — what's the term?
Heptarchy: Seven kingdoms of Anglo-Saxon England. The number of kingdoms and sub-kingdoms fluctuated rapidly during this period as competing kings contended for supremacy.

Houthis: Shia Islamist organization in Yemen.

Indian National Congress: Political party in India.

Alfonso VI of León and Castile

Traditionally dominated by Jerusalem, this mountainous region of the Levant was renamed Syria Palaestina by the Romans after the Bar Kokhba revolt — what was it called?
Judea: Region in the Levant. The name is derived from the Hebrew name Yehudah, and was used during the Babylonian, Persian, Hellenistic, and Roman periods.
Leading a 1980 military coup that deposed Turkey's prime minister and abolished its parliament, this general later served as the country's 7th president — who was he?
Kenan Evren: 7th President of Turkey from 1982 to 1989.
Worshipped as the eighth avatar of Vishnu and central to the Mahabharata and Bhagavad Gita, this major Hindu deity's birthday is celebrated as Janmashtami. Who is he?
Krishna: Major deity in Hinduism. The anecdotes and narratives of Krishna's life are known as Krishna Lila.

After his first wife, heir to the British throne, died in childbirth, this prince — offered the Greek crown following that country's war of independence — instead became first king of a newly independent European nation in 1831. Who was he?
Leopold I of Belgium: King of the Belgians from 1831 to 1865.

The only surviving son of Charlemagne and Hildegard, this Frankish co-emperor conquered Barcelona from the Emirate of Córdoba in 801 and briefly lost his throne for several months in 833–834. Who was he?
Louis the Pious: Emperor of the Carolingian Empire from 813 to 840.
Crowned after his father Alp Arslan died from battle wounds in 1072, this Seljuk ruler saw the empire reach its peak, though real power lay with vizier Nizam al-Mulk — who is he?
Malik-Shah I: Sultan of the Seljuk Empire from 1072 to 1092.
The son of Jupiter and Juno, this Roman deity oversaw both war and farming, and gave his name to the month that begins the campaigning season — who is he?
Mars (mythology): Roman god of war, guardian of agriculture.
This king of Sparta went to war after his wife Helen fled to Troy with the prince Paris, fighting alongside his brother Agamemnon — who was he?
Menelaus: King of Sparta, husband of Helen of Troy. In Greek mythology, Menelaus (Ancient Greek: Μενέλαος, Menélaos) was a king of Sparta.
Kentucky's longest-serving senator in state history, holding his seat since 1985, also became the longest-serving Senate party leader the country has ever had — who is he?
Mitch McConnell: American politician and attorney (born 1942)
Ruling twice as Ottoman sultan — first from 1421 to 1444, then again from 1446 until his death in 1451 — who was this 15th-century monarch?
Murad II: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire (r. 1421–1444, 1446–1451)

After seizing power in a 1961 coup, this South Korean army officer ruled as president until his assassination in 1979, presiding over rapid economic growth — who was he?
Park Chung Hee: President of South Korea from 1963 to 1979.
Possibly descended from Aegean migrants who settled Canaan's southern coast around 1175 BC, this Iron Age people organized their territory into a confederation of city-states — who were they?
Philistines: Ancient people who inhabited Canaan's southern coast.
This Macedonian Greek general, one of Alexander the Great's most trusted companions, retrieved his leader's body after his death and founded a new ruling dynasty in Egypt — who is he?
Ptolemy I Soter: Pharaoh of Egypt from 305 to 282 BC.
This Cuban revolutionary succeeded his brother as president in 2008 and served as the country's defense minister for nearly five decades — who is he?
Raúl Castro: President of Cuba from 2008 to 2018.
Abrasive and reactionary, this right-wing populist and economic nationalist served as New Zealand's 31st prime minister from 1975 to 1984 — who was he?
Robert Muldoon: Prime Minister of New Zealand from 1975 to 1984. After a troubled childhood, Muldoon served as a corporal and sergeant in the army in the Second World War.

On a single 1929 day in a Chicago garage, seven men were lined against a wall and gunned down — some of the killers disguised as police — in a brutal flashpoint of Prohibition-era gang warfare. What is this killing known as?

Saint Valentine's Day Massacre: 1929 gang shooting in Chicago. The Saint Valentine's Day Massacre was the murder of seven members and associates of Chicago's North Side Gang on Saint Valentine's Day 1929.

This wave of mass production, standardization, and rapid scientific discovery, sometimes dubbed the Technological era, is generally dated between 1870 and the outbreak of World War I in 1914. What period was this?

Soul: In religion and philosophy, immaterial essence of a living being.
A London School of Economics graduate from a wealthy family, he led Togo from its 1958 election to independence as prime minister and then president, until his 1963 assassination — who was he?

Sylvanus Olympio: President of Togo from 1960 to 1963. After World War II, Olympio became prominent in efforts for independence of Togo and his party won the 1958 election, making him the prime minister of the country.
Founded by Aleister Crowley in the early 1900s, this occult philosophy centers on discovering one's 'True Will' and the maxim 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law' — what is it?
Thelema: New religious movement founded by Aleister Crowley.

Elected by Ostrogothic nobles in 541 after his two predecessors were killed for trying to surrender to the Romans, this penultimate Gothic king reversed the tide of the Gothic War and recovered nearly all of Italy by 543 — who was he?
Totila: King of the Ostrogoths from 541 to 552.
Meaning 'conclusion of the Vedas,' this orthodox school of Hindu philosophy interprets three core texts known as the Prasthanatrayi — what's it called?
Vedanta: One of the six orthodox traditions of Hindu philosophy.
This Warring States-era Chinese general commanded conquests of three rival kingdoms and is remembered by tradition as one of the four greatest generals of the late Warring States period — who was he?
Wang Jian (Qin): 3rd century BC Chinese military general.

October 1973: the holiest day of the Jewish calendar collided with the 10th day of Ramadan when Arab forces launched a surprise attack on Israel. What war broke out?
Yom Kippur War: 1973 war between Israel and Arab states.

Eric Weinstein is a mathematician. Eric Ross Weinstein (born October 26, 1965) is an American investor and podcast host.
What is the atomic number of Unbinilium?
Unbinilium, also known as eka-radium or element 120, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has symbol Ubn and atomic number 120.
What is the atomic number of Arsenic?
Arsenic is a chemical element; it has the symbol As and atomic number 33.
In what year did Ted Kaczynski die?
Ted Kaczynski: The FBI used the case identifier UNABOM (University and Airline Bombing) before his identity was known, resulting in the media naming him the "Unabomber".
In what year was Angelman syndrome discovered?
Angelman syndrome (AS) is a rare genetic disorder that affects approximately 1 in 15,000 individuals.

Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-19: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. The Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-19 (Russian: Микоян и Гуревич МиГ-19; NATO reporting name: Farmer) is a Soviet second generation, single-seat, twinjet fighter aircraft.
Yakovlev MC-21: United Aircraft Corporation. The aircraft made its maiden flight on 28 May 2017 from Irkutsk.
Who is credited with discovering Lynx?
Lynx (constellation): Johannes Hevelius. Lynx is a constellation named after the animal, usually observed in the Northern Celestial Hemisphere.
Who is credited with discovering Newton's law of universal gravitation?
Newton's law of universal gravitation: Robert Hooke. This is a general physical law derived from empirical observations by what Isaac Newton called inductive reasoning.
Who is credited with discovering Pulsar?
Pulsar: Jocelyn Bell Burnell. This produces a very precise interval between pulses that ranges from milliseconds to seconds for an individual pulsar.
Who is credited with discovering Coma Berenices?
Coma Berenices: Conon of Samos. Coma Berenices is an ancient asterism in the northern sky, which has been defined as one of the 88 modern constellations.
A "classic organochlorine" insecticide once heavily used to treat seed and soil, it was banned in most countries by the 1990s after proving a persistent, bioaccumulating pollutant. What is it?
Aldrin is an organochlorine insecticide that was widely used until the 1990s, when it was banned in most countries.
Named for the Portuguese word for indigo shrub, this simplest aromatic amine smells of rotten fish, ignites into a smoky flame, and is a key precursor to polyurethane and dyes — what compound is it?
Aniline (From) is an organic compound with the formula C6H5NH2.

Around 1920, when the energy source of stars was a complete mystery, which English astrophysicist boldly and correctly guessed it was the fusion of hydrogen into helium — and lent his name to a natural ceiling on a star's brightness?
Arthur Eddington (28 December 1882 - 22 November 1944) was an English astrophysicist and mathematician.

An Arctic and sub-Arctic cetacean, it is one of two living members of the family Monodontidae and is also known as the white whale (the only cetacean regularly occurring with this color) and the sea canary for its high-pitched calls. What is it?
Beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas), is an Arctic and sub-Arctic cetacean.

This semi-solid tissue inside the spongy portions of bones serves as the primary site of new blood cell production in birds and mammals, making up roughly 5% of an adult human's body mass — what tissue is it?
Bone marrow is a semi-solid tissue found within the spongy (also known as cancellous) portions of bones.
Its three-dimensional shape mimics adenosine closely enough to plug into the same receptors, blocking the brain's signal to wind down — which psychoactive substance is it?
Caffeine is a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant of the methylxanthine class and is the most commonly consumed psychoactive substance globally.

A cultivated variety of the same species as cabbage and broccoli, this vegetable's edible part is a dense head of undeveloped flower buds called the curd — one variety, Romanesco, grows its curds in stunning fractal spirals. Name this vegetable?
Charted in 1756 by Lacaille and named for the drafting tool that draws circles, this faint southern constellation is easily confused with the mariner's-compass constellation Pyxis. Which one is it?
Circinus is a small, faint constellation in the southern sky, first defined in 1756 by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille.
This inorganic compound's blue crystalline pentahydrate form was historically called blue vitriol, while its anhydrous form is white and dissolves in water to form an octahedral complex. What is it?
Copper(II) sulfate is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula CuSO4.
Born at the Point McLeay Mission in 1872, this preacher and inventor who registered 10 patents is widely credited as the first Aboriginal Australian published author — who is he?
David Unaipon was an Aboriginal Australian preacher, inventor, and writer who has been widely credited as the first Aboriginal published author.
Fossils of this Late Devonian armored fish genus, among the earliest vertebrate apex predators ever, have turned up from Morocco to Poland to North America — which genus?
Dunkleosteus is an extinct genus of large arthrodire ("jointed-neck") fish that existed during the Late Devonian period, about 382-358 million years ago.

Often used to keep blood pressure from dropping during anesthesia, this stimulant has also been tried against asthma, obesity, and even narcolepsy — though it's no longer the preferred fix. What is it?
Ephedrine is a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant and sympathomimetic agent that is often used to prevent low blood pressure during anesthesia.
This type of anaerobic metabolism harnesses the redox potential of reactants like glucose to produce ATP without needing oxygen. What process is it?
Fermentation is a type of anaerobic metabolism that harnesses the redox potential of the reactants to make adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and organic end products.

Lasting anywhere from milliseconds to hours, these are the most luminous explosions in the universe after the Big Bang, sometimes triggered when massive stars collapse into black holes — what are they?
Gamma-ray burst (GRBs) are extremely energetic events occurring in distant galaxies that represent the brightest and most powerful class of explosion in the Universe.

Dating back roughly 250 million years to the early Triassic, these ground-dwelling herbivorous insects use powerful hind legs to leap away from danger and hatch as nymphs that molt five times — what's the insect?
Grasshopper are a group of insects belonging to the suborder Caelifera.
This naturally occurring molecule and medication is a powerful blood anticoagulant used to treat heart attacks and prevent clotting in dialysis machines and test tubes — what is it?
Heparin (UFH), is a medication and naturally occurring glycosaminoglycan.
In organisms whose total cell count is fixed at maturity, this cell-enlargement process drives nearly all further growth after the embryonic stage — what is it?
Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of individual cells.

In 1897, this British physicist showed that cathode rays were made of previously unknown negatively charged particles far smaller than atoms — the first subatomic particle ever identified. Who was he?
J. J. Thomson (18 December 1856 - 30 August 1940) was a British physicist.
This 19th-century French mathematician ranged across number theory, complex analysis, and mathematical physics — and his name now sits on a crater on the Moon. Who was he?

Joseph Liouville (24 March 1809 - 8 September 1882) was a French mathematician who worked on a number of different fields in mathematics, including number theory, complex analysis, and mathematical physics.
This broadly distributed genus of spiders is informally grouped under a nickname referencing marital loss, encompassing both black and brown members — what is its scientific name?
Latrodectus is a broadly distributed genus of spiders informally called the widow spiders, with several species that are commonly known as the true widows.
Prized as one of the most profitable seafood commodities in the coastal waters where it's caught, this clawed crustacean spends its life in crevices and burrows on the sea floor - which creature?
Lobster are malacostracan decapod crustaceans of the family Nephropidae or its synonym Homaridae.
Its bell-shaped flowers give way to yellow or orange berries, but this nightshade genus is better known by the folkloric root that inspired countless myths and superstitions — which genus?
Mandragora (genus) is a plant genus belonging to the nightshade family (Solanaceae).
This scientific field studies Earth's atmosphere and short-term weather phenomena, with a central focus on forecasting — name the discipline?
Meteorology is the scientific study of the Earth's atmosphere and short-term atmospheric phenomena (i.e., weather), with a focus on weather forecasting.
These small, non-vascular, flowerless plants form dense green clumps or mats in damp, shady spots — name this group of plants?
Moss are small, non-vascular flowerless plants in the taxonomic division Bryophyta sensu stricto.
This form of vitamin B3 is taken orally to treat pellagra without the skin-flushing side effect of niacin, and used as a cream to fight acne and reduce signs of aging skin — what's the compound?
Nicotinamide (INN, BAN UK) or niacinamide (USAN US) (IUPAC name: 3-pyridinecarboxoamide) is a form of vitamin B3 found in food and used as a dietary supplement and medication.
This flowering herb in the mint family, native to the Mediterranean, is sometimes called wild marjoram and is a staple of countless savory dishes. What is it?
Oregano (Origanum vulgare) is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae.
First domesticated in Neolithic China and rarely living past twenty years, this deciduous fruit tree also produces a smooth-skinned variety commercially sold as a different fruit — which tree?
Peach (Prunus persica) is a deciduous tree that bears edible juicy fruits with various characteristics.
Whether captured electronically on a sensor or chemically on light-sensitive film, this art and practice of recording light also powers science and manufacturing — think photolithography. What is it?

Photography is the art, application, and practice of creating images by recording light, either electronically by means of an image sensor, or chemically by means of a light-sensitive material such as photographic film.
This autonomic nervous system disorder causes an abnormally large jump in heart rate — thirty beats per minute within ten minutes — simply from sitting up or standing. What condition is it?
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is a condition characterized by an abnormally large increase in heart rate upon sitting up or standing.
One of America's top rocketry and high-speed-flight experts, this engineer helped found engineering cybernetics before being deported to China in 1955. Who was he?

Qian Xuesen (December 11, 1911 - October 31, 2009; also spelled as Tsien Hsue-shen) was a Chinese aerospace engineer and cyberneticist who made significant contributions to the field of aerodynamics and established engineering cybernetics.
With Patrick Steptoe and Jean Purdy, this British physiologist pioneered the technique that led to the 1978 birth of Louise Brown, earning a 2010 Nobel Prize. Who was he?
Robert Edwards (physiologist) (27 September 1925 - 10 April 2013) was a British physiologist and pioneer in reproductive medicine, and in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) in particular.
Spanning continents from North America to temperate Asia, this genus covers the majority of the world's common bushy-tailed squirrels — which genus?
Sciurus (or) contains most of the common, bushy-tailed squirrels in North America, Europe, temperate Asia, Central America and South America.
About 0.01% of people are born with this condition, in which the heart typically ends up on the right side of the chest instead of the left — what is it?
Situs inversus is a congenital condition in which the major visceral organs are reversed or mirrored from their normal positions.
Also known as sea stars, roughly 1,900 species of these star-shaped marine invertebrates live on seabeds from warm tropics to icy polar oceans. What are they?
Starfish are a class of marine invertebrates generally shaped like a star polygon.
A staple corm across African, Caribbean, Oceanian, and Asian cultures, this root vegetable of the arum family is often likened to yams — what is it?
Taro (Colocasia esculenta) is a root vegetable.

Sitting at the organizational level between individual cells and a full organ, this biological term for a functional grouping of similar cells derives from a French word meaning 'to weave' — what is it?
Tissue (biology) is an assembly of similar cells and their extracellular matrix from the same embryonic origin that together carry out a specific function.

An oily, amber-colored liquid that's extremely non-volatile and therefore lingers in the environment, this organophosphorus compound was developed for chemical warfare and is lethal in doses of just tens of milligrams — which chemical agent?
VX (nerve agent) is an extremely toxic synthetic chemical compound in the organophosphorus class, specifically, a thiophosphonate.

This American physical chemist built ultra-sensitive Geiger counters and once worked on the Manhattan Project — but his 1960 Nobel came for a dating method that revolutionized archaeology and paleontology. Who was he?

Willard Libby (December 17, 1908 - September 8, 1980) was an American physical chemist noted for his role in the 1949 development of radiocarbon dating, a process which revolutionized archaeology and palaeontology.
The first Muslim scientist to win a Nobel Prize, this Pakistani theoretical physicist shared the 1979 Physics prize for unifying the weak and electromagnetic forces — who was he?
First flown in October 1972, this was the world's first twin-engine wide-body airliner, born from a 1967 France-West Germany-UK collaboration that later lost its British partner — what is it?
Airbus A300: World's first twin-engine widebody jet airliner.
Sold under the brand name Xanax, this fast-acting benzodiazepine is most often prescribed for panic disorder and generalized anxiety — what drug is it?
Alprazolam: Benzodiazepine medication. Alprazolam is most commonly prescribed in the management of anxiety disorders, especially panic disorder and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD).
Likened to a bubble or balloon, this outward bulge forms at a weak spot in a blood-vessel wall and grows ever more dangerous as it risks rupture — what is it?
Aneurysm: Bulge in the wall of a blood vessel. An aneurysm is an outward bulging, likened to a bubble or balloon, caused by a localized, abnormal, weak spot on a blood vessel wall.
Also known as pirarucu or paiche, this native of the Amazon River basin is among the largest freshwater fish on Earth — what species is it?
Sold under the brand name Strattera, this selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor treats ADHD and is only recommended for patients age six and up — what is this medication?
Atomoxetine: Medication used to treat ADHD.
A blood-feeding parasite of the genus Cimex that usually bites at night, this insect leaves itchy welts but, reassuringly, isn't known to spread any infectious disease — what is it?
Bed bug: Type of insect that feeds on human blood.

Also nicknamed 'buffalo gnats' or 'turkey gnats,' these small biting insects in the family Simuliidae feed mainly on nectar, though females also drink blood from birds and mammals — what are they called?
Black fly: Family of insects. Black flies or blackflies (sometimes called buffalo gnats, turkey gnats, or white socks) are flies in the family Simuliidae of the Culicomorpha infraorder.

This rare and potentially fatal illness comes from a toxin better known by its cosmetic nickname; it starts with blurry vision and slurred speech but usually spares both fever and consciousness — what is it?
First proposed after the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese, this psychological theory says people are less likely to help a victim when others are present — what's it called?
Bystander effect: Social psychological theory. Recent research has focused on "real world" events captured on security cameras, and the coherency and robustness of the effect has come under question.
Tetravalent and able to form four covalent bonds, this element known since antiquity ranks as the fourth most abundant in the universe by mass — which one is it?
Carbon: Chemical element with atomic number 6 (C)

Greek for "head-feet," fishers nickname these inkfish for their ink-squirting trick; their arms are muscular hydrostats modified from the primitive molluscan foot. Which marine class includes the octopus, squid, and nautilus?
Cephalopod: Class of mollusks. The study of cephalopods is a branch of malacology known as teuthology.
Sold as Thorazine, this drug was the first of the typical antipsychotics — used to treat schizophrenia and, oddly, hiccups that won't quit. What is it?
Their 'lady' actually refers to the Virgin Mary, and their cheerful red-and-black warning colours tell predators they taste terrible — what is this 6,000-species family of small beetles?
Coccinellidae: Family of beetles. The more than 6,000 described species have a global distribution and are found in a variety of habitats.
First created near Darmstadt in 1996 and named for an astronomer on his 537th anniversary, this synthetic element (number 112) is so volatile it may even be a gas — which element?
Copernicium: Chemical element with atomic number 112 (Cn)
Sold under trade names like Super Glue and Krazy Glue, this fast-acting adhesive family rapidly polymerizes the moment it contacts water — which chemical group?
Cyanoacrylate: Type of fast-acting adhesive. The cyanoacrylate group in the monomer rapidly polymerizes in the presence of water to form long, strong chains.
Often called eczema, this term covers skin inflammation marked by itchiness, redness and rash — sometimes with tiny blisters, sometimes thickening over time. What is it?
Dermatitis: Inflammatory disease of the skin.
Developed from the civilian DC-3 airliner and nicknamed 'Dakota' by the RAF, which WWII transport plane hauled troops, cargo, and paratroopers for roughly 100 countries' militaries?
Douglas C-47 Skytrain: Military transport aircraft derived from DC-3.

Defined by permanently erect fangs at the front of the mouth and ranging from a 7-inch white-lipped snake to a nearly 19-foot king, which snake family includes most of the world's neck-flaring venomous serpents?
Elapidae: Family of venomous snakes. The family includes 55 genera with around 360 species and over 170 subspecies.

This Irish experimental physicist shared the 1951 Nobel with John Cockcroft for splitting the atom — the first nuclear transmutation, as the prize committee put it, "entirely under human control." Who was he?
Introduced to North America as early as 1840, this large eusocial wasp builds paper-like nests and preys on beetles, other wasps, and dragonflies — which insect is it?
European hornet: Species of wasp. The European hornet (Vespa crabro) is the largest eusocial wasp native to Europe.
This antiandrogen medication lowers DHT production by about 70 percent and is used to treat pattern hair loss and an enlarged prostate — which drug?

Finasteride: Antiandrogen medication. Finasteride, sold under the brand names Proscar and Propecia among others, is a medication used to treat pattern hair loss and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).

This German chemist won a Nobel Prize for inventing a process that synthesizes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen gas — a breakthrough that today supports nearly half the world's food production. Who is he?
Also known as cranesbills for their pointed seed pods, this 422-species genus bears five-petaled, often veined flowers and includes at least one protocarnivorous species — what's the genus?
A U.S. Navy rear admiral who helped develop COBOL, this computer science pioneer wrote what's considered the first computer manual and worked on the Harvard Mark I — who is she?
Grace Hopper: U.S. naval officer and computer scientist (1906–1992)
Occurring in any of the senses, this perception feels completely real despite the absence of any actual external stimulus — what is it?
Hallucination: Perception that only seems real.
Some called egrets and others bitterns, these 75 species of long-legged, long-beaked wading birds make up the family Ardeidae — what are they?
Heron: Family of birds. The OED also observes that shiterow or shederow are terms used for herons, and also applied as derogatory terms meaning a thin, weakly person.
A colorless, flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odor, this N2H4 compound foams polymer plastics, fills airbag gas generators, and serves as a storable spacecraft propellant. What is it?
Hydrazine: Colorless flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odor. It is a simple pnictogen hydride, and is a colourless flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odour.
Powered by four Aviadvigatel turbofans and built in Voronezh, this Soviet-designed wide-body jet now serves mainly as the Russian president's aircraft — which airliner?
Ilyushin Il-96: Russian four-engined long-range wide-body jet airliner.
A Harvard chemistry professor who studied chlorophyll and helped develop poison gas in WWI, he later became Harvard's president and the first U.S. ambassador to West Germany — who is he?
Nicknamed "Marvellous Merchiston," this 16th-century Scottish laird discovered logarithms and popularized the decimal point — who was this mathematical wizard?
A biologist and botanist married four times — her last husband directed the Manhattan Project's Los Alamos lab — she was played by Emily Blunt in a 2023 film. Who was she?
Its lens-shaped seeds, usually two to a pod, are split and simmered into the dal that's a staple across the Indian subcontinent — which legume?
Lentil: Species of plant with edible seeds.
Nicknamed "Connie" and instantly recognizable by its triple tail and dolphin-shaped fuselage, which four-engined airliner was the first civil aircraft family to widely use a pressurized cabin?
Lockheed Constellation: Family of US airliners with 4 piston engines, 1943.
This age-related eye disease gradually damages the retina's central region, with a 'wet' form involving leaking blood vessels and a 'dry' form marked by deposits called drusen — what is it?
Macular degeneration: Vision loss due to damage to the macula of the eye.

Endemic to North America and known for long, upward-curving upper tusks with little to no lower tusks, this proboscidean's genus split from other elephant relatives at least 28 million years ago — which ancient beast?
Sold under the brand Glucophage, this first-line oral medication for type 2 diabetes is favored partly because it isn't associated with weight gain. What drug is it?
Metformin: Medication used to treat diabetes.

Also called 'selective sound sensitivity syndrome,' this disorder causes specific sounds to trigger strong negative emotional and physiological reactions, though it isn't yet listed in the DSM-5-TR — what is it called?
Misophonia: Disorder of decreased tolerance to specific sounds.
Native to the Americas from Texas down to Argentina, this domesticated waterfowl species has also gone feral in New Zealand, Australia, and parts of Europe — which species?
Muscovy duck: Species of bird. The Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata) is a species of duck native to the Americas, from the Lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas and Mexico south to Argentina and Uruguay.
A cable-like bundle of axons wrapped in three layers of connective tissue, this structure carries electrochemical signals called action potentials — what is it?
Nerve: Cable-like bundle of axons. The axons are bundled together into groups called fascicles, and each fascicle is wrapped in a layer of connective tissue called the perineurium.
This burrowing, semiaquatic South American rodent munches river-plant stems and was shipped worldwide by fur farmers, only to become a destructive invasive pest — which animal is it?
Nutria: Semi-aquatic rodent from South America.
In young children it can mean ear-pulling, extra crying, and poor sleep; it's a group of inflammatory diseases of the middle ear, from acute infections to lingering fluid. What's the medical name?
Otitis media: Inflammation of the middle ear. One of the two main types is acute otitis media (AOM), an infection of rapid onset that usually presents with ear pain.
Found in mice, cats, birds, humans, and dogs but absent in whales and most reptiles, this triangular bone is the body's largest sesamoid — what is it?
Patella: Kneecap, bone covering knee joint.
Known on the street as 'angel dust,' this dissociative anesthetic acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist and can cause hallucinations and psychosis — what is this drug?
Phencyclidine: Dissociative hallucinogenic drug, mostly used recreationally.
Native to Eurasia and temperate Africa but now naturalized worldwide, this flowering plant shares a common name with a banana-like fruit despite being unrelated to it — which species?
Plantago major: Species of flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae.
Covering the front part of the frontal lobe, this brain region orchestrates higher-order thinking including focus, decision-making, and impulse control — what is it?
Prefrontal cortex: Part of the brain responsible for personality, decision-making, and social behavior.
Named by the medieval scholar Gerard of Cremona, this black-looking opening in the eye's iris is round in humans but a vertical slit in cats and a horizontal bar in goats — what is it?
Pupil: Part of an eye. The pupil is a hole located in the center of the iris of the eye that allows light to strike the retina.
Native to western Europe and known scientifically as Ribes rubrum, which widely cultivated berry has escaped into the wild across many regions?
Redcurrant: Flowering plant species in the family Grossulariaceae.
This British economist, who won the 1991 Nobel and spent decades at the University of Chicago Law School, urged the field to study real-world wealth creation in Adam Smith's spirit — who was he?
Ronald Coase: British economist and Nobel laureate (1910–2013)
First known as a portrait painter, this American inventor helped develop a single-wire telegraph system and lent his name to the dot-and-dash code introduced in 1837 — who is he?
Samuel Morse: American inventor and painter (1791–1872)

Nicknamed the 'last Soviet citizen' for being aboard Mir when the USSR dissolved, this cosmonaut flew six missions and helped connect the first Russian and American modules of a space station — who is he?
Sergei Krikalev: Soviet and Russian cosmonaut (born 1958)
This big cat of the genus Panthera prowls the alpine zones of Central and South Asia at elevations of 3,000 to 4,500 meters, from the Himalayas to southern Siberia — what is it?
Snow leopard: Species of large felid.

Named after the patron saint of sailors, this luminous blue or violet glow appears around masts, spires, or aircraft during a strong electric field and can warn of an imminent lightning strike — what is this phenomenon called?
St. Elmo's fire: Luminous plasma created in an electric field.
Occurring in our galaxy roughly once every 61 years, though the last confirmed sighting was back in 1604, this luminous stellar explosion can briefly outshine an entire galaxy?
Encompassing everything from the electrical telegraph to modern radio, this field is defined as the transmission of information over distance using electrical or electronic means — what field is it?
Telecommunications: Transmission of information electromagnetically. The physical limitations of metallic media prompted the development of optical fibre.
Also called T4, this hormone produced by the thyroid gland acts as a precursor to the more active T3 and helps regulate metabolism, heart function and bone health — what is it?
Thyroxine: Thyroid hormone. It is the primary form of thyroid hormone found in the blood and acts as a prohormone of the more active thyroid hormone, triiodothyronine (T3).
Named for its three-lobed shape, this extinct marine arthropod left over 22,000 fossilized species behind after roughly 270 million years in ancient oceans. What creature is it?
Trilobite: Class of extinct, Paleozoic arthropods.
Native to Europe and southwestern Asia, this herbaceous perennial is the type species that lends its name to an entire genus of flowering plants — what is it?
Valerian (herb): Species of flowering plant. Valerian (Valeriana officinalis) is an herbaceous perennial flowering plant in the family Caprifoliaceae, native to Europe and southwestern Asia.
In quantum mechanics, this idea captures how photons and electrons can act like discrete billiard-ball-like objects in some experiments and like spreading ripples in others — what is it?
Wave–particle duality: Concept in quantum mechanics. It expresses the inability of the classical concepts such as particle or wave to fully describe the behavior of quantum objects.
Spread mainly by the oriental rat flea, this gram-negative bacterium caused the Black Death and the Plague of Justinian — what is it?
Yersinia pestis: Species of bacteria, cause of plague.
The symbol for caesium is Cs. Caesium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cs and atomic number 55.
The symbol for livermorium is Lv. Livermorium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lv and atomic number 116.
